Recap of Derivatives
Notation for a full derivative involving x…
y(x)=x^{2}\implies \frac{dy}{dx}=y^{\prime}=2x
Notation for a full derivative involving t…
y(t)=t^{3}\implies \frac{dy}{dt}=\dot{y}=3t^{2}
Types of derivative…
\frac{d}{d(...)}:\text{full derivative}
or…
\frac{\partial}{\partial(...)}:\text{partial derivative}
When differentiating a variable, the other variable(s) are treated as constant:
\begin{align*}
f(x,y)=x^{2}y\implies &\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=2xy,\\
&\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=x^{2}
\end{align*}
In terms of t…
\begin{align*}
f(x,t)=xt\implies&\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=t,\\
&\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}=x
\end{align*}
But what would be the total derivative of f(x,t) with respect to t? Keep in mind that whilst x is a variable, it can be expressed in terms of t (and hence as a function x=x(t)). Total derivative = rate of change if all variables can change.
\frac{df}{dt}\equiv\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot\frac{\partial x}{\partial t}
This equivalence is essentially made up of partial derivatives treating each thing as a variable whilst keeping another constant, but ensuring the result still stays in the form \frac{(...)f}{(...)t}. It’s like you’re adding all the changes up for every variable in order to calculate how much change the entire function has, with respect to a single variable.
\begin{align*}
\frac{df}{dt}&=\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot\dot{x}\\
&=x+t\dot{x}
\end{align*}
Note: How do we tell the difference between partial and total derivatives when the notation is in the form \dot{x}?
f(x,y,t)\implies \frac{df}{dt}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot\frac{\partial x}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot\frac{\partial y}{\partial t}
This pattern for a full derivatives extends continually for additional variables. Note: What other notation is there in different languages, like French?
\begin{align*}
f(x,\dot{x})=x\cdot\dot{x}^{2}\implies&\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=\dot{x}^{2}\cdot\frac{\partial x}{\partial x}=\dot{x}^{2}\\
&\frac{\partial f}{\partial \dot{x}}=x \frac{\partial(\dot{x}^{2})}{\partial x}=x\cdot2\dot{x}
\end{align*}
\begin{align*}
f(x,\dot{x})=x\cdot\dot{x}\implies \frac{df}{dt}&=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot\frac{\partial x}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial \dot{x}}\cdot\frac{\partial \dot{x}}{\partial t}\\
&=\dot{x}\cdot\dot{x}+x\cdot\ddot{x}\\
&=\dot{x}^{2}+x\cdot\ddot{x}
\end{align*}
(the first term with respect to t is omitted, since it’s equal to 0)
Note: figure out a better way to type partial derivatives in LaTeX - it’s so annoying

Recap of Newton Mechanics
Energy E=T+U: the sum of the kinetic and potential energy, respectfully.
Kinetic Energy (scalar and vector)…
for a particle of mass m: T=\frac{mv^{2}}{2}
for two particles of masses m_{1},m_{2}: T=T_{1}+T_{2}=\frac{m_{1}v_{1}^{2}}{2}+\frac{m_{2}v_{2}^{2}}{2}
for a particle of mass m moving along x (where everything is moving →, including a unit vector \hat{i}:|\hat{i}|=1): \vec{v}\equiv \dot{x}\hat{i}, T=\frac{m\dot{x}^{2}|\hat{i}|^{2}}{2}=\frac{m\dot{x}^{2}}{2}.
for two particles of masses m_{1},m_{2} moving along x (where everything is moving →, including a unit vector \hat{i}:|\hat{i}|=1): T=T_{1}+T_{2}=\frac{m_{1}\dot{x_{1}}^{2}}{2}+\frac{m_{2}\dot{x}_{2}^{2}}{2}.
Potential Energy (gravity and spring)…
for a mass m a distance h from the Earth’s surface: U=mgh:g \text{ is a constant}.
for masses m_{1},m_{2} distances h_{1},h_{2} from the Earth’s surface: U=U_{1}+U_{2}=m_{1}gh_{1}+m_{2}gh_{2}.
for a spring compressed with a change in length \Delta{x}: U=\frac{1}{2}k(\Delta x)^{2},\text{ where }k \text{ is a constant}, or if \Delta x is not given, then it can be calculated by calculating the original length of the spring and subtracting its final length ((x_{2}-x_{1})-l): U=\frac{1}{2}k(x_{2}-x_{1}-l)^{2}.

Generalised co-ordinates and degrees of freedom.
By definition, if co-ordinates completely define a position then they are generalised co-ordinates.
Often denoted by q_{i}, where i is the index.
Equal to the number N of degrees of freedom, \text{d.f.}
For a particle in one-dimension, there is one degree of freedom (1\text{d.f.}) since it can only move along one axis, x, hence 1\text{g.c.}
For a particle in two-dimensions (on a plane), there are two degrees of freedom (1\text{d.f.}) since it can move along two axes, x and y, hence 2\text{g.c.}.
Note: the generalised co-ordinates here are x and y, but they’re also often denoted simply as q_{1} and q_{2}. This allows for higher dimensions than x,y,z allows - again, this is hinting towards the mathematical nature of this module.
For a particle in three-dimensions (in a volume)… you get the idea. Three degrees of freedom (3\text{d.f.}) along q_{1},q_{2},q_{3}.
These co-ordinates do not need to be Cartesian, for example they could be polar co-ordinates:
in two dimensions, (r,\theta) have 2\text{d.f.} and hence 2\text{g.c.}:q_{1},q_{2}.
in three dimensions (spherical co-ordinates), (r,\theta,\phi) have 3\text{d.f.} and hence 3\text{g.c.}:q_{1},q_{2},q_{3}. insert funny haha about modelling the physics of spherical horses
These definitions hold for all co-ordinate systems, for N dimensions, where the co-ordinate system will have (N) \text{d.f.} and (N) \text{g.c.} with q_{1},q_{2},\ldots,q_{i}. Note that this is for a single particle - for n particles, the system would have (nN) \text{d.f.}.

Constraints - particle limitations on position or velocity.
Holonomic constraints - can be expressed by the equation f(q_{1},\ldots,q_{s},t)=0, i.e. a function dependent on generalised co-ordinates and time which is equal to zero.
If constraints can not be expressed in this way, they are non-holonomic.
Note that we focus on holonomic, I assume because of the complexity increase when solving differential equations that are equal to a non-zero function.
For example…
a one-dimensional rod stretching between x_{1} and x_{2} (hence with length l=x_{2}-x_{1}) can be expressed as x_{2}-x_{1}-l=0 and thus as f(x_{1},x_{2})=0. Therefore we can conclude the constraint is holonomic.
Another example…
a two-dimensional rod stretching between (x_{1},y_{1}) and (x_{2},y_{2}) (hence with length l^{2}=(x_{2}-x_{1})^{2}+(y_{2}-y_{1})^{2}) can be expressed as (x_{2}-x_{1})^{2}+(y_{2}-y_{1})^{2}-l^{2}=0 and thus as f(x_{1},x_{2},y_{1},y_{2})=0. Therefore we can again conclude the constraint is holonomic.
Note: the absence of time is okay, it’s simply equal to 0.
N particles with p holonomic constraints has degrees of freedom (\text{d.f.}):
one-dimension: n=N-p
two-dimensions: n=2N-p
three-dimensions: n=3N-p
etc.
This makes sense extending the logic before, as each constraint restricts the movement of a particle by one “axis”. Remember, the degrees of freedom is just a numerical value of how much the particles can move in a system.

Organised/University-of-Lincoln/Bachelor.title: MTH2007 Lagrangian Mechanics Cheat Sheet
Organised/University-of-Lincoln/Bachelor.content:
MTH2007 Lagrangian Mechanics - Cheat Sheet


                  
                  Made by William Fayers :) 
                  
                

This all makes a lot more sense if you read and use it before the exam (it’s organised fairly logically though) - practise with it! It assumes knowledge from Differential Equations and Linear Algebra, so revise those too.


Recap of Assumed Knowledge

Solving First-Order Differential Equations: For \frac{dy}{dt} + P(t)y = Q(t), the solution is y(t) = \frac{1}{\mu(t)} \left( \int \mu(t) Q(t)\,dt + C \right), where \mu(t) = e^{\int P(t)\,dt}.
Solving Second-Order Differential Equations: Find the difference between the complementary and particular functions, revise this if you don’t understand what that means.
Doing Integration by Parts uses the formula \int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du. This is useful when integrating the product of two functions, especially when one function simplifies upon differentiation.
Simplify Trigonometric Equations: Use the following identities…

\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1,
\sin(2x) = 2\sin x \cos x,
\cos(2x) = 1 - 2\sin^2x = 2\cos^2x - 1 = \cos^2x - \sin^2x,
\sin a \pm \sin b = 2\sin\left(\frac{a \pm b}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{a \mp b}{2}\right),
\cos a + \cos b = 2\cos\left(\frac{a + b}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{a - b}{2}\right),
\sin\theta \approx \theta:\theta \ll 1,
\cos\theta \approx 1 - \frac{\theta^2}{2}:\theta\ll1.


A Matrix Transpose, M^{T}, is defined as flipping the elements of a matrix over its diagonal: (M^{T})_{ij} = M_{ji}.

The Harder Bits
First decide whether it’s…

A system involving discrete particles - individual masses, like a pendulum or particles;
or a system involving rigid bodies - solid objects with mass distributed continuously which maintains it shape, like a spinning top or rigid rotating mass;
or a system involving a mass in a central field - an individual mass in a force field which points centrally and only depends on distance.

Depending on this, there are different types of question that could be asked:
1. Discrete Particles
1.1 Problem Setup

Identify the system (collection of point masses, e.g. pendulums or particles) and contraints (e.g. fixed distances, surfaces, or other restricting relationships).
Choose generalised co-ordinates…

Count the degrees of freedom, \text{d.f.}=\text{total co-ordinates}-\text{constraints}.
Select the simplest co-ordinates (e.g. angles for rotational systems), q_{1},q_{2},\ldots,q_\text{d.f.}.
Handle multiple dimensions by calculating each component separately and then combine (e.g. x, y, z components).


Define a reference frame: set the origin somewhere convenient (like the point of rotation or a point with fixed constraints) and orient the axes to exploit system symmetry if possible.

Whenever possible, use an inertial frame (no acceleration).



1.2 Possible Question: Finding the Center of Mass or Reduced Mass
The center of mass (\vec{R}) is a point which the whole system can be modelled by. It’s found by taking the average mass-distance of all the particles in each axis, \vec{R} = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{i} m_i \vec{r}_i, e.g. \vec{R}=(\frac{1}{M} \sum m_{i} x_{i},\frac{1}{M} \sum m_{i} y_{i},\frac{1}{M} \sum m_{i} z_{i}), where M is the total mass, m_{i} is the ith mass, and r_{i} is the ith distance from the origin.
Note that the reduced mass (\mu) is similar, but without distance. For example, a two-body problem has \mu = \frac{m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}.
1.3 Possible Question: Moments of Inertia
The moment of inertia (I) measures how a body’s mass is distributed relative to an axis of rotation, affecting its resistance to rotational acceleration. For a system of discrete particles: I = \sum_{i} m_i r_i^2, where r_i is the perpendicular distance from the rotation axis to the i-th particle.
Finding the perpendicular distance will often involve trig, like Pythagoras, or even working out the area of the triangle in two ways (i.e. as given and then rotated).
1.4 Possible Question: Finding Equations of Motion
1.4.1 Express Kinetic and Potential Energy

Kinetic Energy (T) is defined as T = \frac{1}{2} \sum\limits_{i}\left(m_{i}\cdot \sum\limits_{j}\dot{q}_{j,i}^{2}\right), e.g. a one-dimensional system with q_{1}=x and one particle would have T = \frac{1}{2} m\dot{x}^{2} = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}.
Potential Energy (V) is defined as V = \sum_{i} V_i(q_i), where V_{i} depends on the system, e.g. under a gravitational field V_{i} = m_{i} g y_{i}=mgh, or in an elastic system V = \frac{1}{2} k (x_{i} - x_{j})^{2}= \frac{1}{2}kx^{2}.

1.4.2 Formulate the Lagrangian
Find the difference between kinetic and potential energy, L=T-V.
1.4.3 Apply the Euler-Lagrange Equations
For each generalised co-ordinate q_{i}, \frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_i}\right) - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i} = 0. This hence requires…

Partially differentiate L with respect to each co-ordinate.
Partially differentiate L with respect to each co-ordinate’s derivative, then differentiate the results with respect to time.

Then, subtract and simplify (use tools from Recap of Assumed Knowledge) the equations - there should be the same number of equations as there are generalised co-ordinates, i.e. degrees of freedom (\text{d.f.}).
1.4.4 Example
For a small angle simple pendulum, L = \frac{1}{2} m l^2 \dot{\theta}^2 - mgl(1 - \cos\theta), which leads to the Euler-Lagrange equation \ddot{\theta} + \frac{g}{l} \theta = 0 and hence the solution \theta(t) = \theta_0 \cos\left(\sqrt{\frac{g}{l}}\, t + \phi\right).
2. Rigid Bodies
2.1 Problem Setup

Identify the system (a rigid body) and contraints (no deformation, so a fixed inter-mass distance).
Choose generalised co-ordinates…

Euler angles (\phi, \theta, \psi),
or angular velocity components (\omega_x, \omega_y, \omega_z).


Define a reference frame: set the origin to be the center of mass, or a pivot point, and align the axes with the principal axes (so that the inertia tensor is a diagonal matrix, since the co-ordinates would be linearly independent).

2.2 Possible Question: Finding the Center of Mass
The center of mass (\vec{R}) is a point which the whole system can be modelled by. It’s found by taking the average mass-distance of the continuous body in each axis, \vec{R} = \frac{1}{M} \int \vec{r} \, dm, e.g. \vec{R}=(\frac{1}{M} \int x \, dm ,\frac{1}{M} \int y \, dm, \frac{1}{M} \int z \, dm).
2.3 Possible Question: Finding Equations of Rotational Motion with Inertia
2.3.1 Define the Inertia Tensor
The inertia tensor \mathbf{I} describes how the mass of a body is distributed relative to its rotation axes, affecting its rotational motion. It’s defined as…
    \mathbf{I} = \begin{bmatrix}
    I_{xx} & I_{xy} & I_{xz} \\
    I_{yx} & I_{yy} & I_{yz} \\
    I_{zx} & I_{zy} & I_{zz}
    \end{bmatrix}
    
where I represents something similar to a moment of inertia, I_{ij} = \int \left( \delta_{ij} r^2 - x_i x_j \right) \, dm, where \delta_{ij} is the Kronecker delta, r^2 = x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_3^2, and x_i are the position components.
For a rigid body aligned with principal axes, the tensor is diagonal:
\mathbf{I} = \begin{bmatrix}
I_{xx} & 0 & 0 \\
0 & I_{yy} & 0 \\
0 & 0 & I_{zz}
\end{bmatrix},
with:

I_{xx} = \int (y^2 + z^2) \, dm,
I_{yy} = \int (x^2 + z^2) \, dm,
I_{zz} = \int (x^2 + y^2) \, dm.

2.3.2 Finding Moments of Inertia
In a continuous rigid body, the moment of inertia is defined as I = \int r^2 \, dm, where r is the distance from the axis. If you already have one and you’re trying to find a parallel one then it’s equal, just adding Ma^{2} (by the Parallel Axes Theorem).
Examples:

Thin Rod of Length L and Mass M:

About center: I = \frac{1}{12} M L^2.
About end: I = \frac{1}{3} M L^2.


Solid Cylinder or Disc of Radius R and Mass M:

About central axis: I = \frac{1}{2} M R^2.


Solid Sphere of Radius R and Mass M:

About diameter: I = \frac{2}{5} M R^2.



Calculating I for a Thin Rod About Its Center:
I = \int_{-L/2}^{L/2} x^2 \left( \frac{M}{L} \, dx \right) = \frac{1}{12} M L^2.
2.4 Possible Question: Finding Equations of Motion
2.4.1 Express Kinetic and Potential Energy

Kinetic Energy (T) is defined as T = \frac{1}{2} M V_{\text{cm}}^2 + \frac{1}{2} \vec{\omega}^T \mathbf{I} \vec{\omega} (the sum of the translational kinetic energy and rotational kinetic energy), where V_{\text{cm}}=0 if there’s no translation (object is just rotating, not moving through space).
Potential Energy (V) is defined as V = V(q_i), e.g. a spinning top V=mgl\cos\theta.

2.4.2 Formulate the Lagrangian
Find the difference between kinetic and potential energy, L=T-V.
2.4.3 Apply the Euler-Lagrange Equations
For each generalised co-ordinate q_{i}, \frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_i}\right) - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i} = 0. This hence requires…

Partially differentiate L with respect to each co-ordinate.
Partially differentiate L with respect to each co-ordinate’s derivative, then differentiate the results with respect to time.

Then, subtract and simplify (use tools from Recap of Assumed Knowledge) the equations - there should be the same number of equations as there are generalised co-ordinates, i.e. degrees of freedom (\text{d.f.}).
3. Motion in a Central Potential Field
3.1 Problem Setup

Identify the central force (a force that points radially and depends only on distance r), \vec{F} = F(r) \hat{r}, e.g. a gravitational force \vec{F} = -\frac{G M m}{r^2} \hat{r}.
Express the system in polar co-ordinates, (r,\theta), where the position is \vec{r} = r \hat{r} and velocity is \vec{v} = \dot{r} \hat{r} + r \dot{\theta} \hat{\theta}.

3.2 Possible Question: Finding Equations of Motion
3.2.1 Calculating Effective Potential
Defined as the sum of central potential V(r) and centrifugal potential \frac{L^2}{2\mu r^2}: V_{\text{eff}}(r) = V(r) + \frac{L^2}{2\mu r^2}, where L = \mu r^2 \dot{\theta} (angular momentum).
Note that thus if you need to graph this, you should graph central potential and centrifugal potential separately, then plot the graph that adds the two.
For example, in gravitational potential, V_{\text{eff}}(r) = -\frac{G M m}{r} + \frac{L^2}{2\mu r^2}.
3.2.2 Effective Potential Analysis
We can see what this effective potential means for the motion, by finding equilibrium positions where \frac{dV_{\text{eff}}}{dr} = 0, then testing if they’re stable (\frac{d^2V_{\text{eff}}}{dr^2} > 0).
For example, if there’s a stable minima, then it’s a bound orbit (stable circular orbit). Otherwise, it could be an unbound orbit (trajectories escaping to infinity).
3.2.3 Modelling Motion
Using Euler-Lagrange equations in polar co-ordinates we can see how r and \theta change over time.

Radial equation is \mu \ddot{r} = \mu r \dot{\theta}^2 - \frac{dV}{dr},
Angular equation is \frac{d}{dt} (\mu r^2 \dot{\theta}) = 0 \implies \mu r^2 \dot{\theta} = L = \text{constant}.

Combining these leads to the radial dynamics \ddot{r} = \frac{L^2}{\mu^2 r^3} - \frac{1}{\mu} \frac{dV}{dr}. For example, in a gravitational orbit, \ddot{r} = \frac{L^2}{\mu^2 r^3} - \frac{G M}{r^2}.
3.2.4 Find Orbit Shape
Solve for orbits by substituting u= \frac{1}{r} to get \frac{d^2u}{d\theta^2} + u = \frac{F(1/u)}{L^2 \mu^2 u^2}, basically converting the radial equation to a form solvable for \theta.
An example is an orbit with gravitational potential (a Keplerian Orbit): \frac{d^2u}{d\theta^2} + u = \frac{G(m_1 + m_2)}{L^2} with solution u(\theta) = \frac{G M}{L^2} \left[ 1 + e \cos(\theta - \theta_0) \right] such that the orbit is elliptical if e < 1, parabolic if e=1, and e\gt1 hyperbolic. Circular if e=0.

Organised/University-of-Lincoln/Bachelor.content:
MTH2008 Scientific Computing LAB1
Objectives

Learn the basics of using Microsoft Visual Studio, or Microsoft Visual Studio Code.
Compile your first C++ program.

Tasks
Task 1: Writing a simple C++ program
Either open/install Visual Studio or VS Code, using guides on Blackboard if required.
Then, create a new project, selecting the Win32 Console Application C++ template, if possible. You can name this new project something simple, like lab1-task1.cpp.
Your new project should start with some simple code, but you can remove that. Instead, replace it with this:
/**
 * @file basic_use-using_cout.cpp
 * @author YOUR NAME (YOUR EMAIL)
 * @brief Explore using the cout statement
 * @version 0.1.0
 * @date 20xx-xx-xx
 *
 * @copyright Copyright (c) 20xx
 *
 */
#include <iostream>
 
 
int main() {
    /* Print a welcome message */
    std::cout << "Welcome to C++ Programming\n";
 
	/* Return 0 to represnt success */
    return 0;
}
Afterwards, you can compile and build the code, checking if any errors occur. If not, then feel free to experiment with the code to see what happens! Hopefully it’ll print Welcome to C++ Programming and then say something like Press any key to continue....
Task 2: Exploring the welcome program
For this task, we’ll break down the program. Make sure to comment the code so you remember!
First of all, comments in C++ are represent with /* or //, but you need to make sure to stay consistent with one style. We’ll use /* for the rest of the course, so we can differentiate between docstrings easier - these are the big block comments like at the start of the welcome program.
This docstring explains to anyone reading it (including any documentation building programs) what the filename is, who wrote it, etc.
Next, we have the include statement: #include <iostream>. This “includes” the package with all of the input/output stream functions, like the std::cout command we used. It’s part of the standard namespace (packages included with a default C++ installation), hence we use the std:: part.
Optionally, we could also include the line using namespace std; so that we don’t have to write std:: repeatedly, but that can cause package conflicts so it’s common practice not to.
The main function then return an int type - these will be explained more in later sessions. This is because the main function always returns 0 or 1 for success or failure, respectively, hence we return 0 at the end to indicate a successful run.
Finally, the cout function stands for character out, which prints out characters to the console with the insertion operator <<, inserting data into the function. All lines then end with a ; to tell the compiler where lines end.

Organised/University-of-Lincoln/Enterpri.title: Competitor Analysis Template
Organised/University-of-Lincoln/Enterpri.content:
Competitor: SOME COMPETITOR
This document aims to answer the following three questions in complete detail and specificity, with references to sources:

Who are SOME COMPETITOR’s customers?
What is SOME COMPETITOR’s complete business model?
What brand messaging does SOME COMPETITOR use?

1. Customers
An explanation of SOME COMPETITOR’s existing customers and customers they aim to reach.

List the industries that SOME COMPETITOR serves.

For each industry, list what they do and highlight the main thing.


List the customers that SOME COMPETITOR serves.

For each customer, state what role and position they have, e.g. mid-level fleet manager.
For each customer, list the outcomes they aim for.

For each outcome, state if SOME COMPETITOR would help.
For each outcome, list what tasks they do towards it.

For each task, list what problems they might have trying to complete it.

For each problem, state why it could occur.
For each problem, if relevant, state how SOME COMPETITOR could help.






For each customer, list the opportunities SOME COMPETITOR could offer, i.e. as a result of helping with the aforementioned problems.



2. Business Model
An explanation of how SOME COMPETITOR makes money, what products or services they offer to do so.
2.1. Value Proposition

List what SOME COMPETITOR offers.

For each offer, state whether it’s a product or service.

For each product or service, state how it is delivered, i.e. in-person, remote, online application, etc.
For each product or service, state what problems they solve (link back to customer examples if possible).

For each solvable problem, state what platform is used to solve it, i.e. web application, advice, programming, prediction report, etc.


For each product or service, state what benefits are gained by using it.




List what technology, methods, and approaches SOME COMPETITOR uses to offer what they offer.

For each bit of technology, method, or approach, state where it’s used in their services and/or products.
For each bit of technology, method, or approach, explain why it’s used by SOME COMPETITOR, i.e. the benefits (cost, speed, flexibility, risk reduction, etc.).
For each bit of technology, method, or approach, state what resources they use, i.e. people, team size, skills, location, etc.



2.2. Complete Business Model

Explain SOME COMPETITOR’s business model:

Explain how SOME COMPETITOR generates profit:

State how SOME COMPETITOR generates revenue, e.g. government contracts, selling vehicles, offering consultancy, finders fees, etc.

State what SOME COMPETITOR charges for products and/or services.

For each charge, state whether it’s a main revenue stream and why.
For each charge, state how SOME COMPETITOR charges for it, i.e. one-time charge for product, on-demand charging for service, recurring charges for service, etc.




State how SOME COMPETITOR loses revenue, i.e. their costs.

For each cost, state how it’s mitigated to improve profit margins.




State how SOME COMPETITOR markets, e.g. trade shows, website traffic, social media advertisements, etc.
State what partners SOME COMPETITOR has, i.e. recurring customers.



2.3. Business Model Canvas
Using information from the previous sections (sections 1, 2.1, and 2.2), complete the Business Model Canvas, explained here. It should be fairly high-level and just an overview of the more detailed information here.
If you wish to do this digitally, I recommend using Excalidraw so that you can just edit the raw file: Business Model Canvas.excalidraw.
If not, then the image linked is very large, so should print off nicely if converted to a PDF of any size.
Note: You could also just complete this with the original diagrams contained here, the only difference is that I renamed things slightly to be less confusing with reference to this document.

3. Brand Messaging
An explanation of how SOME COMPETITOR communicates its brand and engages with customers through storytelling.

Organised/University-of-Lincoln/Enterpri.title: Enterprise Project Briefing
Organised/University-of-Lincoln/Enterpri.content:
Task 
                  
                

We would like you to perform a competitor analysis for us. This will involve looking at how Lone Star Analysis (LSA) presents itself online compared to its competitors, then creating actionable suggestions regarding the online presence of LSA.


Five Phases of the Project (over 8 weeks)
Phase 1: Project Kick-off
A presentation at the University of Lincoln followed by questions.


                  
                  HINT
                  
                

Familiarise yourself with Lone Star Analysis (LSA) before the meeting! To do this, create a Initial Impressions of Lone Star Analysis document.


Assign roles, discuss timelines, the results of the projects, the methods to reach these results, etc. - all discussed in the Enterprise Project Meeting 0 notes.
Phase 2: Identification
Lone Star Analysis (LSA) will provide an initial list of example competitors, as well as the following points of competition to discuss:

Problems they compete to solve.
Solutions they compete to provide.
Employees they compete to hire.
Brands they compete to build.
Locations they compete to work within.

Based on these points, you should perform a thematic analysis of the LSA website and any other online presence LSA has. Using this analysis, research a long-list of other potential competitors to analyse, with reasoning, to then present to LSA and short-list competitors to focus on.
Phase 3: Analysis
Meet with Lone Star Analysis (LSA) to choose appropriate analysis approaches (framework/techniques/methods relevant to Phase 2’s points of competition).


                  
                  HINT
                  
                

Do some reading and research before the meeting!


Use these analysis approaches to research potential analysis tasks and questions, such as:

What is LSA’s search engine optimisation (SEO) like for its role in the UK and how does this relate to competitors?
What does LSA’s online presence look like on places like YouTube and LinkedIn?
How does LSA’s employee benefits compare to competitors?
What is the feel of LSA’s website? Modern, professional, defence, boring, etc.?

These questions will be mainly answered with independent research, subject matter experts (SMEs) could be approached for help and/or guidance.
LSA will then hold a mini workshop to “Collect, Choose, Create, and Commit” to the set of analysis questions.
After this, you should use the chosen analysis questions/approaches to compare and contrast the online content of three companies, of LSA’s choosing, from the short-list created in Phase 2. Focus on the aforementioned points of competition.
Phase 4: Recommendations
List actionable recommendations that Lone Star Analysis (LSA) can implement to improve or change the website and the rest of their online presence. These recommendations should focus solely on this online presence, not their business or operations.
Prioritise this list for impact against effort to complete.
Phase 5: Findings and Recommendations Workshop
Lone Star Analysis (LSA) and the University of Lincoln (students) will hold a second mini-workshop on analysis and recommendations, where you’ll focus on capturing and documenting LSA’s views on impact, feasibility, and timelines.
Phase 6: Presentation
To conclude to Enterprise Project, you’ll present your analysis finding, suggestions, and mini-workshop discussions, where the specific structure of the accompanying document should be agreed with LSA.
If LSA deems the document to be useful, then the project is a success.

Organised/University-of-Lincoln/Enterpri.title: Enterprise Project Reflection
Organised/University-of-Lincoln/Enterpri.content:
SECTION ONE: Reflection on Project Experience
My group met the objectives well, following the structured phase approach. We familiarised ourselves with LSA during the kick-off phase before identifying some competitors to focus our research on: we wanted to document competitors (and LSA) comprehensively so that we could easily compare the documents and see what LSA is missing from the market standard, as well as how to stand out. After identifying these competitors and writing these documents, we analysed common themes and conducted a detailed competitor analysis report.
Personally, I chaired meetings, prepared agendas, and facilitated many group discussions to progress our goals. I also planned all of our documents, outlining everything so that each member could contribute with minimum initial effort (since everything was already clear and instructed). I also planned timelines and organised the structure of the report, as well as editing the final report to be coherent/comprehensive. After the report, I designed the slideshow and roughly planned each slide so that the group could get some momentum to finish off with.
I developed my existing project management and team co-ordination skills, practising my communication/collaboration abilities during our meetings and shared document work. I also enhanced my analytical thinking somewhat when completing the competitor analyses and engaging in direct discussion with LSA. Beyond all of this, though, I think the most important thing I learned was how to interact with professionals across fields and smaller skills related to this.
I learned that I thrive in organisational and leadership roles, gaining confidence in managing complex tasks and motivating team members. However, in the future I’d focus more on offloading some management aspects and experiment with a less leading role - in the group I was within though, I strongly felt that some leadership/management was missing and the group wouldn’t make much cohesive progress, so I took the role despite this.

SECTION TWO: Application of Project and Life Skills
I applied the presentation skills from the workshop(s) to effectively communicate findings to LSA throughout the project, as well as the final presentation. Moreover, I used insights from the personalities workshop to understand team dynamics further so I could motivate and influence members of the group with more ease. In the future, I can leverage these persuasive communication skills in similar ways along basically any career path, adapting my communication style to suit diverse team members for better collaboration. I’ll continue developing my project management skills for leading and executing projects, too.
Overall, the workshops provided a toolkit of skills for my personal and professional growth which definitely prepared me to tackle future challenges with confidence and competence.

Hard to find UK subsidiary, led to confusion as to what the correct website is.

In the About Us it states that “Since 2004, organisations have trusted Lone Star to deliver actionable answers to complex problems in manufacturing, aerospace, defence, energy, logistics, transportation, and more. Lone Star’s current European client roster includes the Norwegian Ministry of Defence (NORMoD) as well as major defence prime contractors and major offshore operators.”, but these feels difficult to read - why not just implement a logo carousel of companies worked with on the home page?
Nine word summary: Provides decision intelligence and engineering solutions using advanced analytics.
Do the homepage images load correctly?
The entire website is made in a way that I have to get through a wall of boilerplate text in order to get the information I want. It’s designed in a modern way, with a hint towards its defence nature, but feels like it was ported from an older version without changing the actual text content.
The “Solutions” header is confusing. Clicking other headers brings you to a dedicated page, but “Solutions” just reloads to active page. Other header issues are things like “Technology” bringing you to the “Software” page.
Advertised core services:

Predictive & Prescriptive Analysis,
Crew Resource Management,
Leadership Training (links to the same site as Crew Resource Management, this is confusing).

Private/TCT/Database-Recommended-Changes.title: Database Recommended Changes
Private/TCT/Database-Recommended-Changes.content:
In transitioning from the legacy database to the new system, several critical functionalities and data structures from the legacy setup must be carefully integrated to ensure seamless continuity and comprehensive data management. One notable area requiring attention is the management of bank holidays. The legacy database employs a dedicated table to store bank holiday information, including specific dates, descriptions, and flags indicating their integration into the calendar. Incorporating a similar Bank Holiday entity into the new database will facilitate accurate scheduling of events, prevent bookings on holidays, and ensure precise calculations for employee leave entitlements and payroll adjustments. It is also important to identify and exclude any duplicate tables, such as tbl_bankholidays2, to maintain database integrity and avoid redundancy.
Employee skills and qualifications represent another significant aspect present in the legacy system. The legacy database meticulously tracks employee competencies through multiple tables, capturing details like skill names, descriptions, governing bodies, grades, acquisition and expiry dates, and associated documentation links. To preserve this level of detail, the new database should introduce Employee Skills and Employee Qualifications entities. These entities should be directly linked to the Employee entity, enabling comprehensive tracking of each employee’s qualifications, compliance with industry standards, and identification of training needs. This enhancement will support robust reporting capabilities and facilitate professional development initiatives within the organization.
The legacy system’s employee induction process is managed through specific tables that outline induction tasks and track each employee’s progress. These tables include task descriptions, completion statuses, comments, and authorization details. Implementing an Induction Module within the new database is essential to mirror this functionality. This module should allow for the definition and assignment of induction tasks, tracking their completion, recording pertinent comments, and ensuring that tasks are authorized by designated personnel. Integrating this module with the Employee entity will streamline the onboarding process, ensuring that all new hires complete necessary induction activities systematically.
Employee performance and development reviews (PDR) are comprehensively handled in the legacy database through tables that record review dates, summaries, scores, achievements, targets, and associated documentation. To retain this functionality, the new database should incorporate a Performance Review Module. This module should facilitate the scheduling and recording of performance reviews, documentation of achievements and targets, and collection of feedback from both managers and employees. Additionally, it should support the attachment of relevant documents and integrate seamlessly with the Employee entity, thereby fostering a structured approach to employee evaluations and professional growth.
Time Off in Lieu (TOIL) management is another critical feature in the legacy system, tracking accruals, usage, approvals, and related details through dedicated tables. Integrating TOIL management into the new database, potentially within the existing Absence or Leave modules, is necessary to maintain accurate records of employee leave balances, authorization statuses, and compensation methods. This integration will ensure that employees’ extra hours are properly accounted for and managed in accordance with company policies and payroll requirements.
The legacy database also meticulously tracks employee work patterns and schedules, including weekly workdays, start and end times, and break durations. To replicate this functionality, the new database should introduce a Work Schedule entity. This entity should support the definition of regular work patterns, accommodate exceptions and modifications, and integrate with timekeeping and payroll systems. By doing so, the organization can effectively manage staffing needs, monitor attendance, and ensure compliance with labor regulations.
Applicant management, including the tracking of interviews and references, is extensively handled in the legacy system through various tables that store applicant details, interview feedback, and reference information. To support ongoing recruitment processes, the new database should either extend the Employee entity or create a dedicated Applicant entity. This addition should facilitate the management of applicant information, scheduling of interviews, recording of feedback, and storage of reference details. Such a structure will enable a streamlined and efficient recruitment workflow, from application submission to hiring decisions.
The legacy system’s nuanced handling of enquiries, encompassing multiple types and stages, necessitates the implementation of a flexible Enquiry Module in the new database. This module should support diverse enquiry types with specific fields, allow dynamic stage tracking, and integrate with other entities such as Employee, ServiceUser, and Client. By doing so, the organization can maintain a unified and adaptable system for managing all enquiries, ensuring that each enquiry is appropriately categorized, tracked, and addressed based on its specific requirements.
Resource management in the legacy database is facilitated through tables that catalog various resources, including training materials and reference documents. To replicate this capability, the new database should include a Resource Library entity. This entity should store diverse resources with relevant metadata, categorize them for easy retrieval, and implement access controls as necessary. Integrating the Resource Library with training and induction modules will enhance the accessibility and organization of essential materials, supporting employee training and operational efficiency.
Alerts and notifications are managed in the legacy system through tables that associate alerts with employees and service users, including details such as alert messages, comments, and active statuses. Incorporating an Alerts and Notifications system into the new database is crucial to ensure that important information is promptly communicated to relevant personnel. This system should allow for the creation and management of alerts linked to various entities, provide mechanisms for displaying notifications to users, and support the categorization and prioritization of alerts to enhance organizational responsiveness and compliance.
The legacy database also handles disciplinary attachments, storing documents related to disciplinary actions through dedicated tables. To maintain comprehensive records of disciplinary processes, the new database should enhance the Disciplinary entity to include the capability to upload and link relevant documents. This enhancement should ensure secure storage, appropriate access controls, and compliance with data protection regulations, thereby supporting transparent and accountable disciplinary procedures.
Timekeeping and attendance tracking in the legacy system rely on tables that define time slots, weekdays, and week numbers, facilitating detailed scheduling and time management. The new database should adopt standardized date and time fields with appropriate data types and implement scheduling modules that incorporate weekdays and customizable time slots. Incorporating calendar functionalities will improve visualization and management of appointments and shifts, ensuring accurate time tracking and organizational planning.
Training and development are managed in the legacy database through tables that define training topics, types, and formats. To support ongoing employee development, the new database should include a Training Module that allows for the definition of training courses, linking of training to employee development plans, scheduling and enrollment in training sessions, and tracking of completion and certification. This module will enhance the organization’s ability to manage and promote continuous learning and professional growth among employees.
Supplier and order management functionalities in the legacy system are handled through tables that store supplier details and manage purchase orders. If procurement is within the scope of the new system, it is recommended to add Supplier and Order entities to the new database. These entities should manage supplier information, track purchase orders and inventory levels, and integrate with expense and resource modules as necessary. This integration will streamline procurement processes, ensuring efficient management of supplies and resources.
The legacy database includes tables dedicated to messaging and communication, enabling internal communication within the organization by storing messages and tracking their acknowledgment statuses. Incorporating a Messaging System into the new database will facilitate effective internal communication, allowing users to send messages, receive notifications, and track message statuses. This system should support targeted communications to roles or individuals and provide read receipts to ensure that important information is disseminated and acknowledged appropriately.
Compliance and regulatory requirements are addressed in the legacy system through tables that store information about governing bodies and regulatory entities. To ensure adherence to industry standards and facilitate compliance reporting, the new database should include a Governing Body or Certification Authority entity. This entity should store details of regulatory organizations, link them to employee qualifications and certifications, and support compliance verification processes, thereby ensuring that the organization remains compliant with relevant regulations and standards.
Calendaring and event management in the legacy database are managed through tables that store event details, types, locations, and associated comments. To enhance the scheduling capabilities of the new system, it is recommended to strengthen the Appointment and Calendar modules. This enhancement should include comprehensive scheduling features, support for various event types and locations, and integration with other scheduling and time management functionalities. Providing calendar views and synchronization options will improve the organization’s ability to manage appointments and events effectively.
Employee inventory and asset management are meticulously tracked in the legacy system through tables that record assets assigned to employees, including details like item names, serial numbers, assignment dates, and return statuses. To replicate this functionality, the new database should introduce an Asset Management Module. This module should link assets to employees, track assignments and returns, and manage asset statuses, ensuring accurate records of company property and facilitating efficient inventory management.
Absence entitlements and leave management in the legacy database are handled through tables that track annual leave allocations, absence types, and leave balances. To maintain accurate records of employee leave, the new database should expand the existing Absence module to include entitlements and balance tracking. This expansion should manage the accrual and usage of various leave types, provide reporting on leave balances, and ensure compliance with employment contracts and labor regulations, thereby supporting effective leave management and employee satisfaction.
Detailed service user activities are recorded in the legacy system through tables that define standard activity texts for appointments. To ensure consistent and efficient documentation of service user interactions, the new database should enhance the Appointment entity to include standard activity templates. This enhancement should allow for the selection and customization of activity texts, improving documentation accuracy and consistency across service user appointments.
In conclusion, the legacy database encompasses a wide array of functionalities that are essential for comprehensive data management and operational efficiency. To ensure a successful migration, the new database must thoughtfully integrate these legacy features, including bank holiday management, employee skills and qualifications tracking, induction processes, performance reviews, TOIL management, work scheduling, applicant tracking, enquiry management, resource and asset management, alerts and notifications, messaging systems, compliance tracking, calendaring, and detailed absence and leave management. By incorporating these elements, the new database will not only preserve the critical functionalities of the legacy system but also enhance the organization’s ability to manage data effectively, support employee development, ensure compliance, and promote operational efficiency.

application_comments.

One-to-many with Employee (manager-employee relationship): An employee (manager) can manage many employees; an employee reports to one manager.
One-to-many with Absence: An employee has many absences; an absence is associated with one employee.
One-to-many with Contract: An employee can have multiple contracts over time; a contract is associated with one employee.
One-to-many with Disciplinary: An employee can have multiple disciplinary records; a disciplinary record is linked to one employee.
One-to-many with Expense: An employee can submit many expenses; an expense is submitted by one employee.
One-to-many with Enquiry: An employee may handle many enquiries; an enquiry is handled by one employee.
Many-to-many with Address via PersonAddress: An employee can have multiple addresses; an address can be linked to multiple persons.
Many-to-many with Vacancy via EmployeeVacancy: An employee (applicant) can apply to multiple vacancies; a vacancy can have multiple applicants.

starting_date.
closing_date.
status_id → VacancyStatus.id.
filled_date (nullable).

Many-to-many with Employee via EmployeeVacancy: A vacancy can have multiple applicants; an employee can apply to multiple vacancies.

Stores attachments, such as those related to enquiries.

Inherit Auditing.
attached_to_id → Attached.id (nullable).
attachment_link (URL or path to the attachment).

Relationships:

Many-to-one with Attached: An attached item can have multiple attachments; an attachment is linked to one attached item.

decline_reason (nullable).

salary_amount.

date.

town.

Private/TCT/Legacy-Database-Differences-.title: Legacy Database Differences and Recommendations
Private/TCT/Legacy-Database-Differences-.content:
Introduction
The migration from a legacy database to a new system offers an opportunity to streamline and enhance data management practices. However, it’s crucial to carefully analyze the legacy database to identify any functionalities or data that should be carried over to the new system. This document provides a comprehensive comparison of the two databases, focusing on features that may need to be added to the new schema to maintain operational continuity.

1. Bank Holidays Management
Legacy Implementation
In the legacy database, there’s a table named tbl_bankholidays that stores information about bank holidays. This table includes fields such as:

BH_ID: The primary identifier for each bank holiday entry.
BHYear: The year the bank holiday falls in.
BHDates: The specific dates of bank holidays.
Description: A description of the bank holiday.
Added2Cal: A flag indicating whether the bank holiday has been added to the calendar.

Additionally, there is a related table:

tbl_bh_name: Holds the names of bank holidays.

Usage
The bank holidays data is likely used to:

Schedule events and appointments by ensuring they don’t fall on bank holidays.
Calculate employee leave entitlements and manage absences.
Adjust payroll processing for holidays.

Recommendation
Include a Bank Holiday entity in the new database to track national and company-specific holidays. This table should:

Store holiday dates and descriptions.
Be linked to scheduling and absence modules to prevent booking on holidays.
Ensure accurate calculations of working days for payroll and leave management.


2. Employee Skills and Qualifications
Legacy Implementation
The legacy database tracks employee skills and qualifications through several tables:


tbl_emp_skill: Contains information about different skills.


tbl_emp_qual: Stores qualification details.


tbl_skill-qual: Links employees to their skills and qualifications, with fields such as:

Skill_ID: Identifier for the skill.
Emp_ID: Employee identifier.
Qual_Type: Type of qualification.
Skill: Name of the skill.
Description: Description of the skill or qualification.
Qualification: Name of the qualification.
Gov_Body: Governing body that issued the qualification.
Grade: Grade achieved.
Up-to-date: Indicates if the qualification is current.
Date_Aquired: When the qualification was obtained.
Expiry_Date: Expiration date of the qualification.
Comments: Additional notes.
doc_Link: Link to certification documents.



Usage
This detailed tracking allows the company to:

Maintain records of employee competencies.
Ensure compliance with industry regulations requiring certain qualifications.
Identify training needs and plan professional development.
Match employee skills to project requirements.

Recommendation
Add entities for Employee Skills and Employee Qualifications in the new database. The schema should:

Link skills and qualifications directly to employees.
Include relevant details such as governing body, acquisition and expiry dates, grades, and documentation links.
Support reporting on skill gaps and qualification renewals.
Enhance the Employee entity to incorporate these attributes.


3. Employee Induction Process
Legacy Implementation
The legacy system includes tables tbl_emp_induction and tbl_emp_inductiontasks to manage the induction process:


tbl_emp_inductiontasks lists all induction tasks, with fields:

InductionTask_ID: Identifier for the task.
TaskDes: Task description.
Active: Indicates if the task is currently in use.



tbl_emp_induction records each employee’s induction progress:

Induction_ID: Unique record identifier.
Emp_ID: Employee identifier.
Task_ID: Assigned task identifier.
Completed_Date: When the task was completed.
Comment: Additional comments.
Auth_By: The person who authorized or verified task completion.



Usage
This allows the company to:

Assign a standard set of induction tasks to new employees.
Track the completion status of each task.
Ensure compliance with onboarding procedures.
Provide a record for auditing purposes.

Recommendation
Implement an Induction Module in the new database that:

Defines induction tasks that can be updated and maintained.
Associates tasks with employees.
Tracks completion dates and comments.
Includes authorization fields to verify task completion.
Integrates with the Employee entity for seamless onboarding management.


4. Employee Performance and Development Reviews (PDR)
Legacy Implementation
The legacy database uses tbl_emp_pdr, tbl_emp_pdr_achievement, and tbl_emp_pdr_target to manage performance reviews:


tbl_emp_pdr contains overall review records:

Emp_PDR_ID: Review identifier.
Emp_ID: Employee identifier.
PDR_Planned_Date: Scheduled date of the review.
PDR_Actual_Date: Actual date conducted.
Next_PDR_Date: Next scheduled review.
PDR_Summary: Summary of the review discussion.
PDR_Score: Overall performance score.
Manager_Approval and Employee_Approval: Approval flags.
file_Path: Link to review documents.



tbl_emp_pdr_achievement records achievements:

PDR_Achievement_ID: Achievement identifier.
Emp_PDR_ID: Linked to the performance review.
PDR_Achievement: Description of the achievement.
Achievement_Date: Date achieved.
Emp_Achieve_Comment and Man_Achieve_Comment: Comments from employee and manager.
Score: Achievement score.



tbl_emp_pdr_target manages future targets:

PDR_Target_ID: Target identifier.
Emp_PDR_ID: Linked to the performance review.
PDR_Target: Description of the target.
Target_Due_Date: When the target should be met.
Emp_Target_Comment and Man_Target_Comment: Comments from employee and manager.
Target_Met: Indicates if the target was achieved.



Usage
These tables allow:

Structured performance evaluations.
Setting and tracking of employee goals and targets.
Documentation of achievements.
Facilitating manager and employee feedback.

Recommendation
Develop a Performance Review Module in the new database to:

Schedule and record performance reviews.
Document achievements and feedback.
Set targets and track progress.
Include fields for scores, comments, and approvals.
Store associated documents.
Integrate with the Employee entity and potentially the Training module for development plans.


5. Time Off in Lieu (TOIL) Management
Legacy Implementation
The table tbl_emp_toil in the legacy database manages TOIL:


Fields include:

ID: Record identifier.
Emp_ID: Employee identifier.
TOIL_Date: Date of TOIL accrual or usage.
Auth_By: Authorizing person.
Reason and Description: Details about the TOIL.
Payback_Type: How the TOIL will be compensated (e.g., time off, pay).
Credit and Debit: TOIL hours credited or debited.
Approved_Decline: Approval status.
Date_Approved_Declined: Date of approval or decline.
DeclineReason: Reason if declined.



Usage
This system tracks:

Accrual of extra hours worked by employees.
Authorization and usage of TOIL.
Balances of TOIL hours.
Integration with payroll if TOIL is paid out.

Recommendation
Incorporate TOIL management into the new database, possibly within the Absence or Leave module:

Define TOIL accrual and usage processes.
Track authorizations, balances, and approvals.
Integrate with scheduling and payroll systems.
Provide clear reporting on TOIL for employees and managers.


6. Employee Work Patterns and Scheduling
Legacy Implementation
The tbl_emp_workpattern table records work patterns:


Fields include:

Work_Pattern_ID: Identifier.
Emp_ID: Employee identifier.
Week_Number: Week of the year.
Work_Day: Day of the week.
Start_Time and End_Time: Working hours.
Break_Min: Break duration in minutes.



Usage
This allows:

Scheduling of employee shifts.
Tracking of working hours for payroll and compliance.
Planning for staffing needs and coverage.

Recommendation
Add a Work Schedule entity in the new database:

Support defining regular work patterns and shifts.
Allow for exceptions and modifications.
Integrate with timekeeping, attendance, and payroll modules.
Provide visibility for both employees and managers.


7. Applicant Management, Interviews, and References
Legacy Implementation
Applicant tracking is managed through several tables:

tbl_app_details stores applicant information.
tbl_interview and tbl_interviewcomments handle interview scheduling and feedback.
tbl_app_ref records references provided by applicants.

Key fields include:

Personal details (names, contact information).
Application status.
Interview details (dates, interviewers, comments).
Reference details (referee contact info, dates, comments).

Usage
These tables allow:

Tracking of applicants separately from employees.
Scheduling and recording interviews.
Collecting and storing feedback from interviewers.
Managing references and verification.

Recommendation
Extend the Employee entity or create an Applicant entity in the new database to manage recruitment:

Include detailed applicant information.
Schedule interviews and record feedback.
Store references and associated communications.
Support the recruitment workflow from application to hiring.


8. Detailed Enquiry Types and Stages
Legacy Implementation
The legacy database has a nuanced structure for managing enquiries:


tbl_enquiery: General enquiries table with fields such as:

Enquiery_ID: Enquiry identifier.
SU_ID: Service User identifier.
Contact_Type: Method of contact.
Enquiery_Stage: Current stage of the enquiry.
Enquiery_Type: Type of enquiry.



Specific enquiry types are stored in tables like tbl_enq_type_1, tbl_enq_type_2, etc., each with fields relevant to that type.


Stages and statuses are managed through tables like tbl_enq_stage, tbl_prospect_status.


Usage
This setup allows:

Categorizing enquiries by type (e.g., service request, employment interest).
Maintaining detailed information specific to each enquiry type.
Tracking progression through different stages.
Providing tailored responses based on enquiry details.

Recommendation
Implement a flexible Enquiry Module in the new database:

Support multiple enquiry types with specific fields.
Allow dynamic stage tracking.
Integrate with other entities like Employee, ServiceUser, and Client.
Provide a unified system for managing all enquiries while accommodating specific needs.


9. Resource Management
Legacy Implementation
The legacy database includes tables for resource management:


tbl_resource_library: Stores resources available, with fields like:

Resource_ID: Resource identifier.
Resource_Name: Name of the resource.
Resource_Comments: Details or instructions.
Resource_Type: Type of resource (e.g., document, video).
Resource_Category: Category or subject area.
Resourse_Link: Link to the resource.
Source_Site: Original source website.



tbl_resource_type and tbl_resource_cat define types and categories.


Usage
This allows:

Centralized management of training materials, templates, or reference documents.
Easy access for employees to required resources.
Categorization for efficient retrieval.

Recommendation
Include a Resource Library in the new database:

Store various resources with relevant metadata.
Categorize resources for easy navigation.
Provide access controls if necessary.
Integrate with training and induction modules.


10. Alerts and Notifications
Legacy Implementation
Alerts are managed through tables like tbl_emp_alerts and tbl_su_alerts:


Fields include:

Alert_ID: Identifier.
Emp_ID or SU_ID: Associated employee or service user.
Alert: Alert message or content.
Person_Comments: Additional notes.
Current: Indicates if the alert is active.



Usage
Alerts are used to:

Notify staff of important information related to employees or service users.
Highlight critical issues or reminders.
Ensure safety and compliance by flagging relevant concerns.

Recommendation
Integrate an Alerts and Notifications system in the new database:

Allow creation and management of alerts linked to various entities.
Provide mechanisms for displaying alerts to users.
Include fields for activation and deactivation of alerts.
Support categorization and priority levels.


11. Disciplinary Attachments
Legacy Implementation
The table tbl_disciplinary_attachments stores documents related to disciplinary actions:


Fields include:

Disciplinary_Attach_ID: Identifier.
Emp_Disciplinary_ID: Linked to a specific disciplinary record.
file_Path: Location of the attachment.
Description: Description of the document.



Usage
This allows:

Storing supporting documentation for disciplinary actions (e.g., warnings, evidence).
Keeping records compliant with HR policies.

Recommendation
Enhance the Disciplinary entity in the new database to include attachment capabilities:

Allow uploading and linking of relevant documents.
Ensure secure storage and access controls.
Maintain compliance with data protection regulations.


12. Timekeeping and Attendance
Legacy Implementation
Tables such as tbl_timeslots, tbl_weekday, and tbl_week_number are used for scheduling and timekeeping:

tbl_timeslots defines time slots for scheduling.
tbl_weekday lists days of the week.
tbl_week_number tracks weeks in the year.

Usage
These tables support:

Detailed scheduling of appointments and shifts.
Time tracking for employees and service users.
Organizational planning.

Recommendation
In the new database:

Use standardized date and time fields with appropriate data types.
Implement scheduling modules that consider weekdays and custom time slots.
Incorporate calendar functionalities for better visualization.


13. Training and Development
Legacy Implementation
Training topics and formats are managed through tables like tbl_training_topics, tbl_trainingtype, and tbl_trainingformat:


Fields include:

Training_Topic_ID: Identifier.
Enq_Type_3_ID: Links to specific enquiry types.
Training_Topic: Topic name.
TrainingType: Type of training.
TrainingFormat: Format (e.g., online, in-person).



Usage
This system allows:

Managing available training programs.
Linking training to enquiries (e.g., training requests).
Organizing training schedules and formats.

Recommendation
Include a Training Module in the new database:

Define training courses, topics, types, and formats.
Link training to employee development plans.
Support scheduling and enrollment in training sessions.
Track completion and certification.


14. Supplier and Order Management
Legacy Implementation
The legacy database includes supplier and order tables:

tbl_supplier: Stores supplier details.
tbl_order_header and tbl_orderline: Manage orders placed with suppliers.

Key fields include:

Supplier information (names, contact details, account numbers).
Order dates, references, statuses, and payment details.
Order line items with quantities, descriptions, costs, and associated employees or service users.

Usage
This enables:

Procurement management for company resources.
Tracking of inventory and supplies.
Linking purchases to specific projects or clients.

Recommendation
If procurement is within the scope of the new system:

Add Supplier and Order entities.
Manage purchase orders and inventory.
Integrate with expense and resource modules if necessary.


15. Messaging and Communication
Legacy Implementation
Messaging features are present in tables like tbl_int_messages and tbl_msg_seen:


tbl_int_messages stores internal messages:

Fields such as Message_ID, To_Role, To_Individual, Message, End_Date, From, and Priority.



tbl_msg_seen tracks when messages have been read by employees.


Usage
This system allows:

Internal communication within the organization.
Targeted messages to roles or individuals.
Tracking message acknowledgment.

Recommendation
Consider incorporating a Messaging System in the new database if internal communication is a requirement:

Enable sending messages within the application.
Provide notifications to users.
Track read receipts and message statuses.


16. Compliance and Regulatory Entities
Legacy Implementation
There are tables related to compliance, such as tbl_qual_govbody:

Governing_Body_ID: Identifier.
Governing_Body: Name of the governing or regulatory body.
Comments: Additional details.

Usage
This information is important for:

Verifying qualifications and certifications.
Ensuring compliance with industry standards.
Maintaining records for audits.

Recommendation
Include a Governing Body or Certification Authority entity:

Store details of regulatory organizations.
Link to qualifications and employee certifications.
Support compliance reporting and verification.


17. Calendaring and Event Management
Legacy Implementation
Tables like tbl_cal_event_2, tbl_cal_event_location, and tbl_cal_event_type handle calendar events:

Store event details, types, locations, and comments.
Include fields for employees and service users involved.

Usage
This system is used for:

Scheduling appointments and meetings.
Managing calendars for employees and service users.
Recording event-specific information.

Recommendation
Strengthen the Appointment and Calendar modules:

Incorporate event types and locations.
Allow for comprehensive scheduling capabilities.
Provide calendar views and synchronization options.


18. Employee Inventory and Assets
Legacy Implementation
The tbl_emp_inventory and tbl_emp_inventory_type tables manage assets assigned to employees:


Track items like equipment, with details such as:

Invent_Type: Type of inventory item.
Date_Issued, Date_Returned: Asset assignment dates.
Quantity, Item_Name, Item_Serial_Number, etc.
Comments: Additional notes on the asset.



Usage
This allows:

Keeping records of company assets issued to employees.
Managing inventory levels.
Tracking asset allocation and returns.

Recommendation
If asset management is required:

Introduce an Asset Management Module.
Link assets to employees.
Track assignments, returns, and asset statuses.


19. Absence Entitlements and Leave Management
Legacy Implementation
Tables like tbl_absence_entitlement and tbl_absence_year manage absence entitlements:

Track annual leave allocations per employee.
Record absences against entitlements.
Fields include Absence_Entitlement_ID, Emp_ID, Absence_Year, Absence_Type, Absence_Hours_Due, etc.

Usage
This system provides:

Calculation of leave balances.
Management of different types of leave (e.g., vacation, sick leave).
Compliance with employment contracts and regulations.

Recommendation
Expand the Absence module to:

Include entitlements and balance tracking.
Manage accrual and usage of various leave types.
Provide reporting on leave balances and forecasts.


20. Detailed Service User Activities
Legacy Implementation
The tbl_su_activity_txt and related tables store service user activities:

Define standard activity texts for use in appointments.
Fields include Activity_ID, BlockType, ActivityText_Short, Activity_Text.

Usage
This supports:

Consistent recording of activities performed during service user appointments.
Easy documentation and reporting.

Recommendation
Enhance the Appointment entity for service users to:

Include standard activity templates.
Allow selection and customization of activity texts.
Improve documentation efficiency and consistency.

Additional CSS
/* Style the whole contact form */
.wpcf7 {
    background-color: #f7f7f7; /* Light gray background */
    border: 2px solid #6d38c1; /* Purple border */
    padding: 20px; /* Add some padding */
    border-radius: 5px; /* Rounded corners */
    max-width: 600px; /* Limit the width of the form */
    margin: 0 auto; /* Center the form */
    display: flex; /* Use flexbox for layout */
    flex-direction: column; /* Stack elements vertically */
    align-items: center; /* Center items horizontally */
}

/* Style input fields and text areas */
.wpcf7 input[type="text"],
.wpcf7 input[type="email"],
.wpcf7 input[type="tel"],
.wpcf7 textarea,
.wpcf7 select {
    background-color: #fff; /* White background */
    color: #000; /* Black text */
    width: 90%; /* Full width */
    max-width: 300px; /* Limit width for inputs */
    padding: 10px; /* Padding inside fields */
    margin-bottom: 15px; /* Space between fields */
    border: 1px solid #ccc; /* Light gray border */
    border-radius: 4px; /* Rounded corners */
    font-size: 16px; /* Font size */
}

/* Styling for checkboxes */
.wpcf7-checkbox {
    display: block; /* Make each checkbox a block element */
    margin-bottom: 10px; /* Add space below each checkbox */
}

/* Specific styling for pronouns to make them narrower */
.wpcf7 select[id*="pronouns"] {
    width: 15%; /* Set a narrower width for pronoun selects */
    display: inline-block; /* Allow them to sit next to each other */
    margin-right: 2%; /* Space between the two pronoun fields */
}

.wpcf7 select[id^="contact-pronouns"]:last-child {
    margin-right: 0; /* Remove right margin from the last pronoun field */
}

/* Styling for the address box */
.address-box {
    border: 1px solid #ccc; /* Light gray border */
    padding: 15px; /* Padding inside the box */
    border-radius: 5px; /* Rounded corners */
    background-color: #f9f9f9; /* Light background color */
    margin-bottom: 15px; /* Space below the box */
}

/* Style the submit button */
.wpcf7 input[type="submit"] {
    background-color: #6d38c1; /* Purple background */
    color: white; /* White text */
    padding: 10px 15px; /* Padding */
    border: none; /* No border */
    border-radius: 4px; /* Rounded corners */
    cursor: pointer; /* Pointer cursor */
    font-size: 16px; /* Font size */
    width: 100%; /* Full width for the button */
    max-width: 300px; /* Limit width for the button */
}

.wpcf7 input[type="submit"]:hover {
    background-color: #5b2eaa; /* Darker shade of purple on hover */
}

/* Style response messages */
.wpcf7-response-output {
    margin: 2em 0.5em 1em;
    padding: 0.2em 1em;
    border: 2px solid #6d38c1; /* Purple border */
    width: 100%; /* Full width for response messages */
    max-width: 300px; /* Limit width for response messages */
    text-align: left; /* Left-align text in response messages */
}

/* Style for different response statuses */
.wpcf7.sent .wpcf7-response-output {
    border-color: #46b450; /* Green for success */
}

.wpcf7.failed .wpcf7-response-output,
.wpcf7.aborted .wpcf7-response-output {
    border-color: #dc3232; /* Red for failure */
}

.wpcf7.spam .wpcf7-response-output {
    border-color: #f56e28; /* Orange for spam */
}

.wpcf7.invalid .wpcf7-response-output,
.wpcf7.unaccepted .wpcf7-response-output {
    border-color: #ffb900; /* Yellow for invalid */
}

/* Style validation error messages */
.wpcf7-not-valid-tip {
    color: #dc3232; /* Red for error messages */
    font-size: 1em;
    font-weight: normal;
    display: block;
    text-align: left; /* Left-align text in validation messages */
}

Unorganised/DVSA-Theory-Test-Results-Rev.title: DVSA Theory Test Results Review (Maicey)
Unorganised/DVSA-Theory-Test-Results-Rev.content:
Multiple Choice Breakdown

1. Road and Traffic Signs (6 marks needed)
Understanding road signs is crucial for safe driving. This includes recognizing regulatory signs, warning signs, and information signs.
An example question would be something like…
Q: What does a triangular sign with a red border indicate?
A: It indicates a warning of a potential hazard ahead.



                  
                  By the way 
                  
                

This is definitely the biggest category! I recommend focusing on this one to start, since it’s also the one you lost the most marks on :))


Flashcards / Video / Test

2. Safety and Your Vehicle (4 marks needed)
Maintaining your vehicle’s safety is essential. This includes regular checks on tire pressure, oil levels, and lighting systems.
An example question would be something like…
Q: What should you verify before embarking on a long trip?
A: Confirm that the tires are adequately inflated, oil levels are sufficient, and all lights are operational.

Notes & Test

3. Maintaining Safety Margins (2 marks needed)
Safety margins involve keeping a safe distance from other vehicles and obstacles to ensure you can stop or manœuvrer safely.
An example question would be something like…
Q: What is the advised stopping distance at 60 mph on a dry road?
A: The stopping distance is roughly 73 meters (240 feet).



                  
                  NOTE
                  
                

I really don’t like this category as it’s remembering a bunch of numbers… Practice it lots!


Notes & Test

4. Awareness of Vulnerable Road Users (1 mark needed)
Understanding the needs of pedestrians, cyclists, and motorcyclists is vital for safe interactions on the road.
An example question would be something like…
Q: What should you do when you notice a cyclist signaling to turn left?
A: Be ready to give them space and avoid overtaking if it poses a risk.

Notes & Test

5. Required Driving Documents (1 mark needed)
Familiarity with essential driving documents, such as insurance, driving license, and MOT certificate, is crucial.
An example question would be something like…
Q: Which document must you have while driving?
A: A valid driving license.

Notes & Test

6. Understanding Other Vehicle Types (1 mark needed)
Recognizing the characteristics and limitations of various vehicle types, including buses, trucks, and motorcycles, is important for safe driving.
An example question would be something like…
Q: What should you keep in mind when driving near a large vehicle?
A: Large vehicles have bigger blind spots and may require more time to stop.

Notes & Test

7. Motorway Regulations (1 mark needed)
Being aware of specific rules and regulations that govern motorway driving is essential for safety.
An example question would be something like…
Q: What is the maximum speed limit for cars on a motorway?
A: The maximum speed limit is 70 mph.

Notes & Test

8. Staying Alert (1 mark needed)
Recognizing the importance of alertness and being aware of signs of fatigue or distraction is crucial for safe driving.
An example question would be something like…
Q: What should you do if you start feeling drowsy while driving?
A: Safely pull over and take a break.

Notes & Test

9. Hazard Awareness (1 mark needed)
Identifying potential hazards on the road and knowing how to respond is key to safe driving.
An example question would be something like…
Q: What is a potential hazard when driving in wet conditions?
A: Reduced visibility and increased stopping distances.

Notes & Test

Practice Schedule

Week 1: Focus on Multiple Choice

Day 1-2: Road and Traffic Signs (30 minutes each day)
Day 3-4: Safety and Your Vehicle (30 minutes each day)
Day 5: Safety Margins (30 minutes)
Day 6: Vulnerable Road Users and Documents (30 minutes)
Day 7: Review all topics (1 hour)


Week 2: Focus on Hazard Perception
Mock Tests

Day 1-2: Watch and practice hazard perception clips (30 minutes each day)
Day 3: Focus on double hazards (30 minutes)
Day 4-5: Review clips that scored low (30 minutes each day)
Day 6: Take a full mock test (1 hour)
Day 7: Review results and focus on weak areas (1 hour)


Week 3: Full Revision
Mock Tests

Day 1-3: Review all multiple-choice topics (30 minutes each day)
Day 4-5: Review hazard perception clips (30 minutes each day)
Day 6: Take another full mock test (1 hour)
Day 7: Final review :)
